segments.voice: Two cousins walk into the same bedroom, a few moments apart. Krishna is asleep in his palace at Dwaraka. Duryodhana arrives first. He takes a fine seat at the head of the bed. Arjuna comes in after him, and stands at the foot of the bed, hands folded. Both have come for the same thing: Krishna's help in the war that now looks likely. Both wait. Krishna wakes, and the first person his eyes fall on is Arjuna. Today a new book of the epic begins, the Udyoga, and it opens with a choice.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE ERRAND.` → `THE HEAD OF THE BED, THE FOOT.` → `WHO IS SEEN FIRST?`

segments.voice: Udyoga is a Sanskrit word for effort, for getting ready. The name fits. This book is all preparation: for peace, if it can be found, and for war, if it can't. It started in Virata's hall, where the families talked it through. Balarama, Krishna's brother, said the Pandavas should ask gently, since Yudhishthira had chosen to play that game. Satyaki answered him hotly. King Drupada said: send an envoy, and gather allies too. So both sides go looking for friends, and both end up at Krishna's bed. Krishna makes them an offer. On one side, a huge army of his own fighting men. On the other, Krishna himself, alone, and he will not take up a weapon in the fight. Arjuna, he says, may choose first. He saw him first, and he's the younger. Arjuna doesn't hesitate. He chooses Krishna, unarmed. Duryodhana is delighted. He gets the army, and he leaves thinking he's won the better half of the bargain. Now think about what each cousin was really asking for. Duryodhana wanted strength he could count. Arjuna wanted the person. And look back at the bedroom. Duryodhana sat at the head, where a guest of rank sits. Arjuna stood at the feet, the way you stand before someone you honor. Nobody in the story says the seat decided it. The story just shows us where each man chose to be, and whose face Krishna saw when he opened his eyes.
screen: `UDYOGA: EFFORT, GETTING READY` · `THE COUNCIL IN VIRATA'S HALL` · `AN ARMY, OR KRISHNA UNARMED` · then, large: `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA`

segments.voice: Settle, and fold your hands, the way Arjuna stands at the foot of the bed. Bring to mind something you're asking for these days, from a person or from life. Breathing in, name it plainly. Breathing out, ask underneath it: is this strength I can count, or a presence I want near? There's no wrong answer. Just let the question rest with your folded hands. If you pray, you can bring the asking into your prayer. The bell holds the time.

screen: `UDYOGA.` · `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: An envoy rides into the Pandava camp. It's Sanjaya, the trusted charioteer and counselor of the blind king Dhritarashtra. He greets everyone warmly, asks after their health, and then delivers his master's message. It isn't an offer. It isn't a threat. It's a plea: don't fight. Notice what's missing from the message. Dhritarashtra asks for peace, but he doesn't offer to give back what was taken. Today, an embassy that talks about peace and leaves out the price.
screen: `SANJAYA RIDES IN.` → `THE MESSAGE: DON'T FIGHT.` → `WHAT THE MESSAGE LEAVES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya speaks movingly, and the Pandavas don't brush it aside. A war between cousins, he says, means killing your own teachers, your own uncles, your own kin. What kind of victory is that? It would be better, he says, to live on alms than to win a kingdom that way. Yudhishthira listens, and his answer is not angry. I want peace too, he says. Who would choose war if peace were possible? But peace has to mean something. Give us back our own kingdom, Indraprastha, the city we built. Krishna speaks as well. Holding back from action, he says, is no answer by itself; a person must act, and act rightly. In Krishna's reply, Sanjaya's advice sounds holy but asks only one side to give anything up. And then, in this same exchange, Yudhishthira makes a request so small it's almost painful to hear. Not the whole kingdom. Not even the city. Give us five villages, he says, and let this end. Five villages, from men who once ruled. Sanjaya carries the message home. And in the next scenes of the book, we'll watch what the Kuru court does with it. Today, just stay with the shape of the exchange. One side talks about peace as the absence of fighting. The other talks about peace as fairness, and is willing to accept very little of it.
screen: `SANJAYA: DON'T FIGHT YOUR KIN` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: WE WANT PEACE TOO` · `KRISHNA: ACT, AND ACT RIGHTLY` · then, large: `EVEN FIVE VILLAGES`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let your breath come and go. Bring to mind a disagreement you're in, at home, at work, with a friend. Just let the two questions sit side by side. If you pray, you can bring that disagreement into your prayer. The bell holds the time.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Sanjaya pleaded for peace, and Yudhishthira asked for five villages. Your line was five villages, and let this end. Did you ask what a fair peace would look like? Day eight hundred fifteen.

segments.voice: Krishna decides to go to Hastinapura himself. One more try for peace, in person. Before he leaves, each of the brothers gives him a message, and several of them lean toward peace. Then Draupadi comes to him. She takes her long dark hair in her hand, the hair Duhshasana dragged her by in the dice hall, and she holds it up. When you speak of peace, she says, remember this. If my husbands won't fight, my old father will, and my sons will. Krishna promises her she'll see justice. Then he sets off. Today, the road to Hastinapura, and a dinner Krishna refuses to eat.
screen: `KRISHNA GOES HIMSELF.` → `DRAUPADI HOLDS UP HER HAIR.` → `REMEMBER THIS.`

segments.voice: Hastinapura gets ready for him. Duryodhana has rest houses built along the road and lays out a great feast. This is diplomacy as hospitality: if Krishna eats at his table, he's half won. Krishna passes the rest houses by. In the city he greets the old king, and then goes to Kunti, the Pandavas' mother, who has been living in Vidura's house all these years. She weeps and asks after her sons, one by one. Only then does Krishna go to Duryodhana's palace. He accepts his greeting, and declines the meal. Duryodhana is offended. Why won't you eat with us? Krishna's answer is short and sharp. A person eats another's food, he says, either out of love, or out of need. You feel no love for me, and I'm in no need. So he walks back to a much plainer house: the home of Vidura, the wise half-brother of the king, the one who spoke up for the Pandavas years ago in the dice hall. That's where Krishna eats, and that's where he stays. Look at what Krishna is doing before he says a word in the assembly. Draupadi's hair goes with him. He won't eat at the table of a man who means harm. He sleeps under the roof of a man who told the truth when it was dangerous. He visits the mother first. An embassy isn't only speeches. It's where you eat, and where you sleep, and whom you visit first.

screen: `UDYOGA.` · `SUPPER AT VIDURA'S.`

segments.voice: Morning in the great hall of the Kurus. Every seat is filled: Dhritarashtra on his throne, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna beside them. Krishna walks in, and the hall goes quiet. This is the moment the whole Udyoga has been building toward: a formal chance to stop the war, spoken face to face, in front of everyone who matters. Today, Krishna's counsel in the Kuru assembly, and what the court does with it.
screen: `THE HALL IS FULL.` → `KRISHNA WALKS IN.` → `A CHANCE TO STOP THE WAR.`

segments.voice: Krishna speaks to Dhritarashtra first, and his argument is simple. You can stop this, he says. Your sons and your nephews could stand together, and no one could stand against them. Peace would be your gain, not your loss. Give the Pandavas their share. Others speak after him. Old sages tell stories of pride brought low. Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to make peace. Duryodhana hears them. And he refuses. He says, in effect, that he won't give the Pandavas even as much land as the point of a needle would cover, and he walks out of the hall. Then Gandhari, his mother, is sent for. He is called back to hear her, and she tells her son plainly that a person who can't rule his own anger and greed can't rule a kingdom. He leaves again. Outside, he and his friends make a plan: seize Krishna, tie him up, and the Pandavas will be helpless. Word reaches the hall. And Krishna laughs. The text says that as he laughed, his body blazed, and gods and heroes seemed to stream out of him, so bright the court had to shut their eyes. Only a few could look: Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the sages, and Dhritarashtra, who was granted sight for that moment. Then the vision ends, and Krishna walks calmly out. The point of the scene isn't only the wonder. It's that Krishna came anyway. The night before, at Vidura's, he said he had come so that no one could blame him for not trying. So he made the whole case for peace in public, where no one could say it was never offered.

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna made the case for peace before the whole Kuru court, Duryodhana refused, and Krishna walked out. Your line was no one could say it was never offered. Did you say one fair thing out loud, even expecting a no? Day eight hundred seventeen.
screen: `KRISHNA'S COUNSEL AT COURT.` · `DURYODHANA REFUSES.`

segments.voice: A chariot rolls out through the gates of Hastinapura. The embassy has failed. Duryodhana would not give the Pandavas their share, and war is coming. Krishna is leaving. But before he goes, he does something odd. He calls Karna, Duryodhana's friend and champion, and invites him up beside him. The two ride out of the city together, away from the crowd. What Krishna says on that ride could stop the war before it starts. It rests on a secret about who Karna's mother is. Today: the ride.
screen: `THE EMBASSY HAS FAILED.` → `KRISHNA CALLS KARNA UP` → `A SECRET ON THE ROAD`

segments.voice: Here is the secret. Karna is Kunti's son, born to her before she married Pandu. That makes him, Krishna says, the eldest brother of the five Pandavas. He doesn't stop at the news. He makes an offer. Come with me. Your brothers will touch your feet. You will be king. Yudhishthira himself will stand behind your throne. Everything Karna has been denied, the rank, the family, the respect, is laid at his feet in one ride. And Karna's answer is the heart of today. He says he already knows. Then he says why it changes nothing. His mother set him adrift as a newborn. A charioteer named Adhiratha found him, and Adhiratha's wife Radha raised him. Karna says her milk fed him and her love kept him alive, and he will not stop being her son for a crown. He married among the charioteer's people. He has children there. And for years Duryodhana has stood by him when no one else would. He gave Duryodhana his word, and he means to keep it. Then he asks Krishna for one thing: don't tell Yudhishthira. If Yudhishthira learned that Karna was his elder brother, Karna says, he would hand him the kingdom, and Karna would hand it straight to Duryodhana. Better that it stays secret. So a man is offered everything he ever wanted, and turns it down for the people who loved him first. Some readers hear loyalty in that. Some hear tragedy. The epic lets you hear both.

screen: `KRISHNA'S OFFER.` · `KARNA STAYS RADHA'S SON.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Ganga, a man stands with his face to the east and his hands raised, reciting his prayers. The sun climbs. It burns the back of his neck, and he doesn't move. Behind him, a woman has come quietly and stands in the shade of his own upper cloth. She waits until he is finished. It's Kunti, and the man is Karna. Yesterday, Krishna asked Karna to change sides. Today, his mother comes to ask the same thing, in person.
screen: `PRAYERS ON THE GANGA BANK` → `KUNTI WAITS IN HIS SHADOW` → `A MOTHER'S REQUEST`

segments.voice: Karna finishes, turns, and greets her by naming himself: I am Karna, son of Radha and Adhiratha. What can I do for you? Hear the sting in that, even if he doesn't intend one. Kunti tells him the truth. You are not a charioteer's son. You are mine, and the Sun's. Come to your brothers. In the text, a voice even speaks from the sun to confirm her words. Karna doesn't doubt her. But he answers her plainly, and it's hard to hear. You cast me away when I was born. You never gave me a mother's care. Now, on the eve of war, you come to me for the sake of your other sons. And then, after the hardest words, Karna gives her something. He will not join the Pandavas. But he makes a promise. In the battle, he will not kill four of her sons: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, even when he has them at his mercy. Only Arjuna will he fight to the end. Either way, he says, you will still have five sons: with Arjuna, or with me. Kunti trembles and embraces him. She asks him to remember his promise, and they part. Look at what has happened in this chapter. The Udyoga book is the book of getting ready, and both sides use it to gather allies. Karna uses it to give away his advantage, out of love for a mother who gave him up. It's a gift, and it may cost him his life.

segments.voice: Settle where you are. Let your shoulders drop. Think of a conversation you've been putting off, one where the truth is hard and the love is real. You don't have to have it today. Just breathe with it. Breathing in, name the hard thing, silently. Breathing out, name the thing you could still give, even if you can't give everything. Stay there, between the two, the way Karna did on the riverbank. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Udyoga. The book of getting ready. Our days with it end here, on choices made by a river, before the armies take the field.
screen: `UDYOGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you will still have five sons. Today, in one place where you can't give everything, give the one thing you can. Day eight hundred eighteen.

819.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is printed and recited on its own, and it is also read in place as part of the Bhishma Parva, where Sanjaya narrates it to the blind king Dhritarashtra.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Udyoga days ended by the Ganga, with Karna's promise to Kunti: four of her sons spared, and you will still have five sons either way. Where did you give the one thing you could? Day eight hundred nineteen.
screen: `KARNA'S PROMISE.` · `FIVE SONS EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: The armies are drawn up on the field of Kurukshetra. In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and waits. Then the sage Vyasa comes to him with an offer. If you want to see the battle, he says, I'll give you sight. Watch it all. And the king says no. He doesn't want to see his own family killed. He only wants to hear about it. So Vyasa gives the gift to someone else: Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counselor. Today the Bhishma book opens, and the Bhagavad Gita, which we've read before, comes back to us inside the story that holds it.
screen: `THE ARMIES ON KURUKSHETRA` → `THE BLIND KING REFUSES SIGHT` → `SANJAYA WILL SEE FOR HIM`

segments.voice: Earlier in the path we read the Gita verse by verse, as a teaching on its own. For these six sessions, we put it back where it lives: in the middle of a war report. And the frame is stranger than it first seems. After Vyasa's visit, the book doesn't go straight to the first morning of battle. Instead, Sanjaya comes back to the palace with terrible news. Bhishma, the grandsire of the whole family, has fallen. Days of fighting have already passed. Dhritarashtra breaks down, and then he asks Sanjaya to tell him everything, from the start. So when the Gita opens with the old king asking what his sons and Pandu's sons did on the field of dharma, he is asking about something already over. He's asking the way someone asks after a funeral: tell me how it happened. Everything Krishna says to Arjuna, every word about duty, about the self that is never killed, about acting without clinging to the result, reaches us through Sanjaya's mouth, spoken to a grieving father who refused to look. That changes how the Gita sounds. It's not a lecture in a quiet hall. It's a conversation reported in a dark room, after the worst news, to a listener who chose to hear rather than see. Over the next five sessions we'll walk through the chariot, the teaching, the vision, and the morning after, all in place.
screen: `THE GITA PUT BACK IN THE STORY` · `THE TELLING STARTS AFTER BHISHMA FALLS` · `A FATHER ASKS: HOW DID IT HAPPEN?` · then, large: `THE GITA, TOLD BY SANJAYA`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or let them rest on the floor. For a moment, be like the king: a listener, not a watcher. Let your breath settle, and turn your attention to sound. The nearest sound. Then something farther. Then the farthest thing you can hear. Don't name them or judge them. Just receive them, the way Dhritarashtra received the whole war through one voice. If you pray, you can let one sound become the start of your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma Parva. The Book of Bhishma, the book of the Mahabharata that holds the Bhagavad Gita inside it. This week carried us from the Udyoga embassy, through Karna's two refusals, to this dark room.
